sections.h2: Where to pay and who to call
sections.html:
Payments go to the City Treasurer's Office inside City Hall at 1155 28th Street SW, Wyoming, MI 49509. The same office bills water, sewer and other city charges. Wyoming is in Kent County, and after March 1 the Kent County Treasurer handles any real property tax still open.

The Assessor's Office tracks about 25,000 parcels, with owner names, mailing addresses, structure photos and sketches, permit lists and transfer histories. Call the assessor at 616-530-7231.

Drivers can use the window behind the building, staffed Monday to Thursday from 7:00 a.m. until 5:00 p.m.

Summer taxes are due August 31 and winter taxes February 14. A late payment costs the following.

Wyoming tax due dates and late penalties
BillDue dateLate penalty
SummerAugust 314% interest added September 1, then 0.5% on the first of every month, up to 6%
WinterFebruary 143% interest penalty added February 15

Unpaid real property tax is handed to the Kent County Treasurer on March 1. Business personal property tax stays with the city, which adds 1% monthly until it is settled.

The summer penalty starts the day after August 31, so if you close near that date, use a title company that confirms which bill it paid.

Wyoming takes payment in person, by mail, through a drop box and online. Cash or a check brought to the Treasurer's Office adds no convenience fee.

  • Online payment runs through Invoice Cloud at wyomingmi.gov/payment. Cards carry 2.7% with a $1.95 minimum, and e-checks cost $0.80.
  • Single card payments top out at $25,000, and e-checks at $125,000.
  • Accepted online: Discover, MasterCard, American Express and Visa, plus PayPal, Venmo and e-checks.
  • For mail, write the check to the City of Wyoming and enclose the stub or account number. A drop box is at the northeast entrance of City Hall.
  • Anything received after 5:00 PM counts the next day. Never mail or drop off cash.

To learn a parcel's balance before closing, call the Treasurer's Office or use the property information link on its page.

The city assesses real property at 50% of its usual selling price, as Michigan law directs. It uses a computer assisted mass appraisal system adjusted with current market data, and it halves true cash value to get assessed value.

The yearly calendar is public. Value notices are mailed on the last Friday of January. Complaints go to the assessor from the first Monday in February to the second Thursday, and the roll is certified on the first Monday in March.

Every parcel appears by address, with current value and last sale price, in five alphabetical street ranges. Check your neighbors' numbers before you file a complaint.

Go to the assessor's review in early February first. Still unhappy? The March Board of Review is where a formal appeal happens. Its executive session falls the day after the first Monday of March, hearings open the second Monday, and every review wraps up by the first Monday of April.

  • The board can raise, lower or confirm a value, put missed property on the roll, and grant principal residence and other exemptions that were missing last year.
  • The July and December meetings fix clerical errors and mutual mistakes of fact. The assessor adds qualified agricultural exemptions, taxable uncappings and hardship exemptions to that list.
  • The Michigan Tax Tribunal is the next step, with filing deadlines of May 31 for commercial and industrial property and July 31 for residential.

City Council appoints board members to three year terms. Each set includes a real estate practitioner, a public accountant and a property owner who has lived in the city at least a year.

Beyond the March appeals, the assessor's calendar has several more dates. February 1 is the deadline for the qualified business form L-4143. February 20 is the deadline for personal property statements (Form 632), small business property tax exemption claims (Form 5076) and the eligible manufacturing personal property affidavit (Form 5278).

  • First Monday in March: the assessor certifies the assessment roll.
  • Wednesday after the first Monday in April: the Board of Review roll goes to Kent County.
  • June 1: principal residence exemption affidavits for the summer bill.
  • November 1: the same affidavits for the winter bill.
  • December 31: tax day, which fixes the condition of a property for the next year's assessment.

A Board of Review looks only at the facts that existed on tax day.

sections.h2: Exemptions and what a sale changes
sections.html:
An owner-occupied home qualifies for the principal residence exemption, which removes up to 18 mills of school operating tax. A buyer must own and live in the home by June 1 to have it on the summer bill, or by November 1 for the winter bill. A later move-in waits for the next tax year. A form may have been signed at closing, and anyone unsure should file one with the Assessor's Office.

Only one such exemption is allowed per person, so the seller's old homestead needs a rescind form before a new one can be granted. A separate disability exemption is claimed on Form 5107 with the federal disability paperwork, and the city asks for a copy of a driver's license.

The buyer owes a transfer affidavit within 45 days. Missing it can bring back tax from the transfer date with penalties and interest. For an existing owner, taxable value is held down by the cap. A sale lifts it to assessed value the following year, so a new owner often sees a larger first bill.

Taxes attach to the parcel, so any open summer or winter bill has to be cleared at closing or credited to the buyer. Call the Treasurer's Office for the balance, and ask the title company which bill it plans to pay. If the property is already with the Kent County Treasurer after March 1, the county office is the one to call.

A cash buyer can close without waiting on a lender's tax review, but the balance still has to be paid from proceeds. File the rescind form for your old homestead exemption so the new owner starts clean.

Wyoming is West Michigan's second largest city after Grand Rapids. Population is 78,588 on 24.74 square miles of land. About 67.1% of homes are owner-occupied, owned homes have a middle value of $225,200, and rent runs $1,196 at the median. The 28th Street retail corridor and the 74 acre former General Motors stamping plant site, now called Site 36, are the main redevelopment focus.

faqs.q: What are the Wyoming, Michigan property tax deadlines?
faqs.a: August 31 for summer and February 14 for winter. Summer picks up 4% on September 1 and a half percent each month after, to a cap of 6%. Winter takes 3% on February 15.

faqs.q: Can I pay Wyoming taxes without going inside City Hall?
faqs.a: Yes. A drive-up window behind City Hall is staffed Monday through Thursday, 7:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. There is also a drop box at the northeast entrance, and online payment carries a fee.

faqs.q: Who gets a Wyoming tax bill after March 1?
faqs.a: The Kent County Treasurer collects delinquent real property tax from that date. Personal property tax stays at the city, with 1% interest each month.

faqs.q: When does a Wyoming owner dispute a value?
faqs.a: Early February for the assessor's review, then the March Board of Review, which opens hearings on the second Monday of March. Residential owners may go on to the Michigan Tax Tribunal by July 31.

faqs.q: Does my homestead exemption follow me from a Wyoming sale?
faqs.a: No. File a rescind form for the old home. The buyer applies for the exemption and qualifies by owning and occupying the house before June 1 for the summer bill or November 1 for the winter.
